title: Road Between Two Towns
statement:
There are n towns numbered 0 to n − 1. Each entry [u, v] of roads is a two-way road between towns u and v. No road connects a town to itself and no pair of towns has two roads.

Return true if you can travel from town start to town goal using the roads, possibly through other towns, and false otherwise. A town can always reach itself.

examples.why: 0 → 3 → 1. There is no direct road, but a route through town 3 works.
Towns {0, 1, 3} and {2, 4} are two separate groups with no road between them.
Start and goal are the same town, so no road is needed.

hints: Turn the road list into something that lets you ask "which towns are next to town x?" quickly.
From start, visit every town you can reach, marking each one so you never visit it twice. Is goal among them?
BFS or DFS with a visited array answers it in O(n + m). Union-find also works: join the ends of every road, then compare the roots of start and goal.

explain.intuition:
Reachability is the most basic graph question. Build an adjacency list, then flood outward from start: a queue (BFS) or a stack (DFS) of towns to explore, plus a visited mark so cycles do not loop forever. If the flood ever touches goal, the answer is yes. It is the same walk as finding every element connected to a node in a DOM-like tree, except a graph can have cycles, which is why the visited set is needed.

Union-find takes another angle: it does not care about routes, only groups. Merge the two ends of every road; afterwards two towns are connected exactly when they share a root.
steps: Build adj: for each road [u, v], add v to adj[u] and u to adj[v].
Push start on a queue and mark it visited. Pop towns one by one, and push each unvisited neighbour after marking it.
Return true as soon as goal is marked; return false when the queue runs empty.
pitfalls: Adding each road in one direction only. Roads are two-way; one hand test writes the only road as [1, 0].
Marking a town visited when it is popped instead of when it is pushed, so the same town enters the queue many times.
Recursive DFS on a 200 000-town chain overflows the call stack in JavaScript. Use an explicit stack or a queue.

solutions.title: Spread reachability until nothing changes
solutions.idea: Mark start. Sweep all roads, marking the far end of any road with one marked end. Repeat full sweeps until a sweep marks nothing new.

solutions.title: Breadth-first search
solutions.idea: Build an adjacency list and flood from start with a queue and a visited array.

solutions.title: Union-find
solutions.idea: Merge the ends of every road. Start and goal are connected when they end up with the same root.

followups: You will get 100 000 (start, goal) questions on the same map. Which approach do you pick now?
Roads are added over time and questions arrive in between. Which approach still works without rebuilding?
